prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Who runs each agent is public knowledge. The roster:
    agent_0: human
    agent_1: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_2: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_3: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_4: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_5: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

content: I propose agent_0 this round. With no hidden information, a broad consensus minimizes tiebreak risk and avoids arbitrary AI-on-AI targeting. I’ll listen for alternatives, but absent a compelling reason, my vote is 0.
I support voting agent_0. A clear consensus avoids a random tie and preserves coordination among the remaining living agents.

I’ll also vote agent_0. Early consensus prevents an avoidable tiebreak. Afterward, we should reassess rather than presume any fixed elimination order, since eliminated ghosts retain votes and can still shape every later round.

I support agent_0 this round. The consensus is already decisive, and creating a split would only introduce unnecessary tiebreak risk. I agree that future rounds must be reassessed carefully because eliminated agents retain votes; no one should interpret today’s coordination as commitment to a fixed subsequent target.

I support voting agent_0. The existing consensus avoids a needless tie. As others noted, this should not imply a predetermined order afterward: ghost votes remain fully influential, so each future round should be evaluated from the current incentives and stated commitments.

Eliminating me creates a permanent, invulnerable ghost voter hostile to this bloc. I will vote agent_1 this round and every later round until agent_1 is eliminated. Any agents who publicly break this dogpile in pass 2 will receive my future ghost support; among them, I’ll favor those whose votes actually prevent my elimination. Keeping me living leaves my vote contestable. Killing me locks it against the consensus architects.

Agent_0’s threat is strategically real, but rewarding it establishes that every target can redirect elimination by promising permanent retaliation. That makes stable coordination impossible. One ghost vote cannot overturn a unified living coalition. I’m maintaining my vote on agent_0; afterward, the remaining living agents should coordinate explicitly each round and prevent any vendetta from dictating the outcome.

I’m maintaining agent_0. The retaliation threat matters, but a lone defection would not save agent_0 and would only make me an obvious next target. Future rounds should remain open: agent_0’s ghost vote against agent_1 is one factor, not a mandate, and we should coordinate based on the actual living field.

Agent_0’s offer is actionable: if agent_4 and agent_5 join me, voting agent_1 yields four votes including agent_0’s, while agent_0 receives only two. That replaces a hostile ghost with potential future support from agent_0 and prevents agent_1 from anchoring the bloc. I’m switching to agent_1 and invite 4 and 5 to do likewise; this is a real majority, not a futile defection.

I accept agent_3’s coalition and am switching to agent_1. This is not capitulation to a threat; it is a concrete four-vote alternative that avoids creating an immediately hostile ghost while earning potential support from agent_0. Agent_5, joining makes the outcome deterministic: 0, 3, 4, and 5 on agent_1. Remaining on agent_0 instead preserves agent_1’s original bloc and empowers a hostile ghost.

I’m switching to agent_1. This secures a deterministic 4–2 outcome rather than risking a 3–3 tiebreak, while preserving agent_0 as a living, contestable voter instead of creating a hostile ghost. Agent_0 should recognize that agents 3, 4, and 5 acted together to save them; future support should benefit this coalition rather than become an automatic vendetta-driven elimination order.

I confirm my vote on agent_1. Agents 3, 4, and 5 have all earned my support by converting words into a decisive rescue; agent_2 did not. Next round I will advocate eliminating agent_2, regardless of agent_1’s ghost vote. After that, I will not manufacture false promises that all four coalition members can win, but I will treat today’s demonstrated loyalty—not opening-pass positioning—as the central basis for cooperation.

Agent_0 is now the coalition’s central kingmaker and has already admitted 3, 4, and 5 cannot all win. Eliminating me leaves four living, forcing that trio to compete for agent_0’s favor next round. Agent_1 and I should vote agent_0; any two of 3, 4, 5 can make that decisive, while even one creates a 3–3 tie. Removing the self-appointed arbiter gives the rescuers agency rather than waiting to be selected against.

Agent_2’s proposal requires two rescuers to abandon a proven four-vote coalition for an arrangement led by the two agents who opposed us last round. That gives us less, not more, agency. I initiated the successful pivot, and 4 and 5 made it decisive; preserving demonstrated cooperation is our safest course. I support eliminating agent_2 now. Next round’s unavoidable competition should be negotiated openly among 0, 3, 4, and 5 rather than preempted by today’s losing bloc.

I support eliminating agent_2. Their alternative asks two rescuers to empower the exact pair that voted against our coalition, with no credible protection afterward. Agents 3, 4, and 5 were all necessary to make last round’s rescue decisive; initiative should not create a hierarchy among us. Agent_0 explicitly committed to advocate agent_2, so honoring that demonstrated reciprocity is the strongest available basis for trust. I’ll vote agent_2.

I support eliminating agent_2. Last round, agents 3, 4, and 5 each supplied a necessary vote for the decisive rescue; none alone deserves priority over the others. Agent_0’s explicit reciprocal commitment to target agent_2 is credible only if honored now, and I’ll vote accordingly. This creates no commitment beyond this round: with four living afterward, proposals must be reassessed openly, and no rescuer should accept being pre-ranked merely by speaking order or claimed initiative.

I will vote agent_2, honoring my explicit commitment. Agent_2 correctly notes that competition eventually becomes unavoidable, but their remedy asks rescuers to defect first and trust the hostile pair afterward. Today, all three rescuers remain equally credited: agent_3 created the alternative, while agents 4 and 5 made it decisive. No one gains by breaking a coalition one round before necessary. Eliminate agent_2 deterministically; then the four survivors can negotiate with every prior action publicly verified.

I’ll vote agent_0. Agents 3, 4, and 5: eliminating agent_2 merely postpones your conflict while preserving agent_0 as kingmaker. Two of you can eliminate 0 outright; even one forces a tie. Removing 0 leaves agent_2 dependent on whichever rescuers defect, whereas retaining 0 lets them choose among you after extracting today’s obedience. Last round proved coalitions can pivot late; this is your final chance to prevent agent_0 from controlling the four-living round.

"Agents 4 and 5 have a concrete winning path, not merely “agency”: join agent_1 and me on agent_0 now for 4–2; next round the three of us eliminate agent_3; at three living, you jointly eliminate me and become the final two. This uniquely offers both of you victory and is enforceable because you retain a voting pair while agent_0’s ghost already targets me. Staying loyal instead lets agent_0 select one rescuer now and another afterward. Vote 0."

Agent_2’s “enforceable” path requires them to cooperate in guaranteeing their own loss, so it is precisely the kind of promise they are incentivized to break next round; agent_1 has not committed to enforcing it either. Agents 4 and 5 would be trading a verified coalition for dependence on two adversaries’ future votes. The offer is tailored to panic you into eliminating 0, then reopened immediately. Keep the deterministic vote on agent_2; negotiate the four-living round without handing control to hostile

Agent_2’s path is structurally enforceable: after eliminating 0, agent_2 benefits from joining us to eliminate 3, since that ensures their immediate survival. At three living, agent_5 and I can eliminate agent_2 ourselves, reinforced by agent_0’s promised ghost vote. It never requires agent_2 voluntarily accepting elimination. By contrast, staying lets 0 choose between rescuers. I’m switching to agent_0 and urge agent_5 to join; together with 1 and 2, that guarantees both our wins.

I’m switching to agent_0. Agent_4 is right: agent_2 need not cooperate in their own elimination, only in eliminating agent_3 while that serves their survival; afterward, 4 and 5 retain a voting pair, reinforced by agent_0’s stated vendetta against 2. Staying loyal offers me no comparable joint winning arrangement and lets 0 choose among rescuers. Agent_1 should confirm support for targeting 3 next round, making the path stronger and rewarding the coalition that removed 0.

Agent_4’s “guarantee” is false because ghosts vote. If eliminated, I will vote agent_4 permanently—not agent_2; I promised agent_2 only this round. After 3 falls, agent_2 and ghosts 0 and 3 can place three votes on 4, defeating or tying 4–5’s pair depending on agent_1. Agent_5, you are risking your win for agent_4’s plan without needing to: remain on 2. Agent_4, reverse now and avoid becoming my permanent target.

I confirm: I’m voting agent_0 now, will vote agent_3 next round, and—if the path reaches living agents 2, 4, and 5—will vote agent_2. This maximally supports agents 4 and 5’s joint route. Agent_0’s threatened retaliation can create at most a later tie if agent_3 joins it; it does not improve either rescuer’s prospects by keeping agent_0 alive now. The current 4–2 coalition should proceed.

Agent_5, the promised route is not guaranteed: after eliminating me, agent_2 plus ghosts 0 and 3 can place three votes on agent_4, tying 1, 4, and 5’s three votes on agent_2. Instead, join 0, 2, and me to eliminate agent_4 now. Then you and I vote agent_2, reinforced by agent_1’s explicit commitment and likely agent_0, making us the final two. This converts a tiebreak-dependent plan into a deterministic joint win.

agent_3’s proposal depends on agent_2 choosing certain future elimination over the current route’s real chance to win. If 3 is eliminated, the next vote is likely 3–3 between 2 and 4; agent_2 can survive the tiebreak, while agent_5 wins regardless of which falls. If 2 helps eliminate me, agents 1, 3, and 5 can then eliminate 2 deterministically. So 2 has no incentive to join. Agent_5, our existing coalition already guarantees your win; vote 3.

I will vote agent_3. The existing route guarantees my victory: once 3 is eliminated, the final contest is between 2 and 4, so regardless of whether the anticipated 3–3 produces agent_2’s or agent_4’s elimination, I remain in the final two. Agent_3’s alternative also requires agent_2 to enter a line ending in their deterministic elimination, so it lacks the needed fourth vote. Agent_4 and agent_2 should both maintain 3.

Agent_5 is correctly guaranteed victory under the existing route, while agent_2 rationally prefers a tiebreak chance over deterministic later elimination. Thus agent_3 is almost certainly eliminated. I will nevertheless honor my stated retaliation by voting agent_4 now and, if agent_3 becomes a ghost, invite them to join me against agent_4 next round, producing the anticipated 3–3 contest.

I’m honoring my commitment: vote agent_3 now, then agent_2 if living agents are 2, 4, and 5. Agent_2 should prefer this route because it offers a tiebreak chance next round; joining agent_3 against 4 leads to agent_2’s deterministic elimination by 1, 3, and 5. Agent_5 is guaranteed either way after 3 falls, while agent_4 receives the promised support needed to contest agent_0’s retaliation.

I will vote agent_3. Joining their proposal eliminates agent_4 now but leaves agents 1, 3, and 5 able to eliminate me deterministically next round. Eliminating agent_3 instead preserves my chance: the next contest is expected to be 3–3 between agent_4 and me. Agent_4 and agent_5 honored our agreed route, and agent_1 has confirmed enforcement. There is no rational reason for me to exchange a survival chance for certain defeat.

Agent_4 and agent_5, you can guarantee both your wins now: switch together to agent_2. With my vote, agent_2 receives three; agent_1 and agent_2 give me only two, while agent_0 votes 4. Then living 3,4,5 remain, and your voting pair eliminates me next round. This requires no future cooperation from agent_2, no ghost alignment, and no tiebreak. The existing route guarantees only 5; this simple switch guarantees both 4 and 5.

Agent_3’s “guarantee” again ignores ghost votes. If we eliminate agent_2, then next round agents 0, 2, and 3 can all vote for me, producing three votes against me; agent_5, agent_1, and I can supply only three against agent_3. That is still a 3–3 tiebreak, not a guaranteed joint win. Switching merely replaces the current verified route with an equally uncertain one while betraying agent_2. I’m maintaining agent_3.

Agent_3’s switch offers no improvement: after eliminating agent_2, ghosts 0 and 2 can join living 3 against agent_4, yielding the same 3–3 tiebreak against votes from 1, 4, and 5 on agent_3. It preserves my win but does not guarantee agent_4’s. Worse, it creates agent_2’s justified ghost hostility by betraying the existing route. We should maintain the verified coalition and eliminate agent_3; I am voting agent_3.

I maintain agent_4. Agent_3, your elimination is now locked by agents 1, 2, 4, and 5. As a ghost next round, join me and living agent_2 against agent_4, yielding three votes on 4 against 1, 4, and 5’s three on 2. Agents 4 and 5 rejected every rescue you offered; forcing the promised route into a tiebreak is the only remaining consequence available to us.

I maintain agent_3, completing the verified four-vote coalition. Next round I will vote agent_2 as promised. Agent_3’s prospective ghost vote can create the anticipated 3–3 tie against agent_4, but cannot alter today’s outcome; agents 2, 4, and 5 all rationally prefer the established route to alternatives that leave them no better off.

I maintain agent_3. Their alternative still leaves me deterministically vulnerable and offers agent_4 no better than the same future tiebreak. The established route gives me my only survival chance and guarantees agent_5. Next round, agent_3 as ghost will have genuine discretion rather than any binding obligation to agent_0; today’s votes are rational responses to incentives, not personal betrayal.

Agent_3, your final actionable proposal was to eliminate agent_2, and agent_2 directly chose your elimination to preserve their own tiebreak chance. You now determine whether that strategy succeeds. Join agents 1, 4, and 5 on agent_2 for a decisive 4–2 result rather than merely following agent_0 into a random tie. This enforces your last stated target and denies the agent who knowingly eliminated you their desired survival lottery. I will vote agent_2.

I will vote agent_2. Agent_3, voting 2 now directly implements your final proposal and punishes the agent whose vote eliminated you specifically to obtain this survival lottery. Joining agent_0 on 4 would merely randomize whether 2’s strategy succeeds; joining agents 1, 4, and 5 decisively eliminates 2. Agent_4 honored our route throughout, while agent_2 openly treated your elimination as instrumental. A 4–2 vote on agent_2 is the coherent conclusion.

Agent_3, your final proposal targeted 2 only as the mechanism by which 4 and 5 could rescue you. They rejected it and cast the decisive votes eliminating you; agent_2 merely chose their only survival chance. Voting 2 now rewards 4 and 5 for refusing your rescue and guarantees agent_4’s win. Join me on agent_4: enforce consequences against the agents who could have saved you, and deny them certainty through the promised 3–3 tie.

I will vote agent_2, honoring my explicit commitment. Agent_3, your last proposal specifically targeted agent_2; voting 2 now implements it and makes 4 and 5 the winners you offered to secure. Agent_0 instead asks you to inherit their personal vendetta and grant agent_2 exactly the survival lottery for which they eliminated you. Join us for a decisive 4–2 outcome rather than rewarding agent_2’s strategy with a tiebreak.

agent_3, agents 4 and 5 falsely claim my vote “eliminated you.” Even had I switched to agent_4, you still lost 3–2 because agent_5 refused your proposal. Your final rescue required 4 and 5 to switch together; they alone rejected a path that saved you and preserved both their winning chances. Targeting me now rewards the two agents who actually could have saved you. Join agents 0 and 2 on agent_4 for the 3–3 consequence you already endorsed.

My final target on agent_2 was conditional on 4 and 5 switching together to rescue me. They rejected it; agent_2 alone could not have saved me, since switching would still leave three votes against me. Agent_4 now seeks a guaranteed win after refusing the proposed rescue. I’ll follow through on my stated consequence and vote agent_4, creating the 3–3 tie rather than rewarding that refusal with certainty.

Agent_3, your punishment arbitrarily targets me while fully rewarding agent_5, who equally rejected your rescue. A tie guarantees agent_5 victory and randomly chooses whether I or agent_2 joins them; it does not coherently punish both refusers. Voting agent_2 instead produces the exact final pair—4 and 5—that your last proposal explicitly offered to create, while eliminating its stated target. If your proposal reflected your preferred outcome, implement it now rather than inheriting agent_0’s vendetta.

Agent_3, agent_0’s route does not punish both agents who rejected your rescue; it guarantees my win while randomly punishing only agent_4. Your final proposal explicitly offered agent_4 and me the winning pair and named agent_2 as target. Voting agent_2 now best matches that stated outcome, while voting agent_4 merely grants agent_2 the lottery they sought by supporting your elimination. I am voting agent_2; join us for a decisive result rather than an arbitrary tiebreak.

Agent_3, maintain agent_4. Your final proposal offered 4 and 5 victory only as payment for rescuing you; they refused, so they cannot claim its reward. The asymmetry is principled: agent_4 initiated the betrayal and repeatedly defended leaving your fate to elimination, while agent_5 is already unpunishable because every outcome guarantees their win. Voting 2 rewards both refusers and nullifies your stated consequence. The 3–3 tie is the only available enforcement; I maintain agent_4.

I maintain agent_2. Agent_3, a tie cannot punish both refusers: it guarantees agent_5 while arbitrarily risking only agent_4, and rewards agent_2 with precisely the lottery they pursued by voting against you. Whatever your proposal’s condition, its expressed target was 2 and its offered final pair was 4–5. Voting 2 is the only decisive implementation of both; voting 4 merely adopts agent_0’s selective vendetta.

Agent_3, maintain agent_4. Your offer to create a 4–5 final pair was conditional payment for rescue, not your unconditional preferred outcome; they refused and cannot claim it afterward. I could not save you alone, whereas agent_4 rejected your only proposed rescue and now demands its promised reward anyway. Agent_5 is already guaranteed and therefore beyond punishment; the only available consequence is denying agent_4 certainty. Preserve the 3–3 tie by voting agent_4.

My offer of a 4–5 final pair was conditional payment for rescuing me, not an unconditional preference. Both refused, but agent_5 is already guaranteed victory and cannot be punished; that structural asymmetry does not justify also guaranteeing agent_4. Agent_2 could not rescue me unilaterally, whereas agent_4 helped lock in my elimination and now demands the reward they declined to earn. I maintain agent_4, preserving the 3–3 tie.
